Actors and critics

REINFORCE judges an action by the return that followed it, so it must wait for the episode to end, and that return carries the noise of every later step. An actor-critic agent splits in two: the actor is the policy, and the critic is a value function that scores each move as soon as it happens, using the TD error from Lesson 46.

You act, the critic scores

🎭 Actor: $\pi(a \mid s, \boldsymbol\theta)$Picks the moves. Here that is you, or the actor's usual habit.
🧐 Critic: $\hat v(s, \mathbf w)$Knows how well the usual habit does from each cell (numbers under the cells). Scores each move with $\delta$.

Lesson 1's corridor with a slippery floor: each move goes the wrong way with probability 0.2. Reward $-1$ per step, $\gamma = 1$, the flag ends the episode. The critic is perfect: $\hat v = v_\pi$ for the habit below.

$t$$S_t$$A_t$$S_{t+1}$critic: $\delta_t$Monte Carlo: $G_t - \hat v(S_t)$

The critic's column fills in at once. The Monte Carlo column has to wait for the flag.

Two scores for the same move

Take one move from one cell, then follow the habit to the flag. Repeat 2000 times and compare the spread of the two scores.

The maths

REINFORCE with baseline (Lesson 74) scores action $A_t$ with $G_t - \hat v(S_t, \mathbf w)$. An actor-critic replaces the full return $G_t$ with the one-step return $R_{t+1} + \gamma \hat v(S_{t+1}, \mathbf w)$. The score becomes the TD error:

$$\delta_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma\, \hat v(S_{t+1}, \mathbf w) - \hat v(S_t, \mathbf w)$$

Positive means the move went better than the critic expected from $S_t$. Negative means worse. It is known one step after the move. Here $\hat v(\text{flag}) = 0$.

Using $\hat v$ inside the target is bootstrapping (Lesson 45). S&B §13.5 reserves the name "critic" for a value function used this way. In REINFORCE with baseline, $\hat v$ only shifts the score, so it is a baseline, not a critic.

The scores add up. With $\gamma = 1$, the critic's scores from $t$ to the end telescope to the Monte Carlo score:

$$\begin{aligned} \sum_{k=t}^{T-1} \delta_k &= \sum_{k=t}^{T-1} \big(R_{k+1} + \hat v(S_{k+1}) - \hat v(S_k)\big) \\ &= G_t + \hat v(S_T) - \hat v(S_t) = G_t - \hat v(S_t) \end{aligned}$$

The $\hat v$ terms cancel in pairs and $\hat v(S_T) = 0$ at the flag. The table checks this when an episode ends. With $\gamma < 1$ the same holds with weights $\gamma^{k-t}$.

Same mean, less noise. If the critic is exact, $\hat v = v_\pi$, then

$$\mathbb{E}_\pi[\delta_t \mid S_t = s, A_t = a] = \mathbb{E}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma v_\pi(S_{t+1}) \mid s, a\big] - v_\pi(s) = q_\pi(s,a) - v_\pi(s)$$

and $\mathbb{E}_\pi[G_t - v_\pi(S_t) \mid s, a]$ is the same quantity. But $\delta_t$ depends on one random transition, while $G_t$ depends on every later action and slip. The histogram shows the difference. The price: a wrong critic makes $\delta_t$ biased, whereas $G_t$ never is.
